{% raw %}
Flow Rescue is a minimal Python + Taichi physics-game demo for the graphics simulation
course project. The player digs through soil to route a finite set of water particles
into the yellow collection area.

This vertical slice now runs a compact 2D Position-Based Fluids loop behind the stable
`FluidSolver.step(dt, terrain)` boundary: external forces, predicted positions, uniform-
grid neighbor search, iterative density constraints, terrain projection, and velocity
write-back.

## Setup

```bash
uv sync
uv run python -m tools.generate_demo_level
```

The repository pins Python 3.12 in `.python-version` and locks all dependencies in
`uv.lock`. `uv sync` creates the local `.venv` and installs both runtime and development
dependencies.

The generated `assets/levels/demo.png` is committed so the demo runs immediately. Run
the generator again after changing the level script.

## Author Levels

Tiled maps in `assets/levels_src` can be imported into the runtime level format:

```bash
uv run python -m tools.import_tiled_level \
  assets/levels_src/level_02_pipe_rescue.tmj \
  --output-dir assets/levels \
  --stem level_02_pipe_rescue
```

The game still loads only generated `assets/levels/*.json` and `*.png` files. See
`docs/level_editor.md` for Tiled layer names, object types, and custom properties.
The player-facing MVP level order and design intent are documented in
`docs/playable_levels.md`.
See `docs/art_direction.md` for the GPT, Doubao, and Claude icon-hero sprite states and UI art direction.

## Run

```bash
uv run python main.py
uv run python main.py --arch cpu
uv run python main.py --arch cpu --mode demo
uv run python main.py --arch cpu --manifest assets/levels/manifest.json
uv run python main.py --arch cpu --level assets/levels/demo.json
uv run python main.py --arch cpu --headless --frames 120
uv run python main.py --arch cpu --level assets/levels/smoke_gameplay_components.json
uv run python main.py --arch cpu --headless --frames 120 --level assets/levels/smoke_gameplay_components.json
uv run python main.py --arch cpu --headless --frames 120 --level assets/levels/smoke_timed_faucet.json
uv run python main.py --arch cpu --headless --frames 120 --level assets/levels/smoke_pipe.json
uv run python main.py --arch cpu --headless --frames 120 --level assets/levels/smoke_hazard_scene.json
uv run python main.py --arch cpu --level assets/levels/smoke_click_faucet.json
```

The default `--arch auto` mode asks Taichi for a GPU backend and allows CPU fallback.
Use the CPU command when verifying a machine without a working GPU path.
Without `--level`, the app loads `assets/levels/manifest.json` and exposes level
selection in the runtime panel. Use `--level` to run one level directly for debugging.
`--mode debug` is the default and shows development panels, smoke levels, and metrics.
`--mode demo` starts on a player-facing level select screen and filters out manifest entries with
`demo_visible: false`.
In manifest mode, the runtime UI supports level selection, current-level restart,
previous/next navigation, and a final completion message after the last visible level.
The visible demo sequence includes five levels covering direct digging, pipe transfer,
timed faucets, click-triggered water, and hazard scene markers.
Debug runtime panels show controls, collection progress, FPS, physics timing, active
particles, and optional solver stats such as PBF iterations and neighbor count.
Press `T` in debug mode to toggle detailed per-phase timing (grid build, constraint
solve, collision, grid overflow); these lines are hidden by default.
Demo gameplay keeps the playfield clear with only a corner pause button; the pause menu offers
exit, retry, and level-select actions. Missing solver stats are shown as `n/a` so the UI
remains usable before the PBF milestone lands.
Completed demo levels show a star-rating result screen with level-select, retry, and
next-level actions when another level is available.

Controls:

- Left mouse button: interact with click components and dig soil
- `Up` / `Down`: move the selection on the demo level-select screen
- `Space`: pause or continue
- `R`: restart the level
- `N`: next level in manifest mode
- `P`: previous level in manifest mode
- `W`: switch between particle and continuous water rendering
- `G`: toggle occupied Uniform Grid overlay in debug mode
- `C`: toggle collider and boundary overlay in debug mode
- `T`: toggle detailed profiler timing in debug mode
- `Esc`: quit

The click-faucet smoke level is manual: click the top source area to emit water.

## Test

```bash
uv run pytest
uv run python -m tools.validate_levels assets/levels
uv run python main.py --arch cpu --headless --frames 120
```

The tests use the CPU backend and cover level loading, coordinate conversion, digging,
terrain reset, gravity, rock-floor collision, uniform-grid neighbors, small-scale PBF
separation, dense-block stability, boundary clamping, corner collision, narrow-channel
flow, goal collection, completion, and restart.

The level validator loads every committed level JSON and PNG pair. Headless runs print
backend, particle capacity, active particle count, collected particles, simulated time,
wall-clock elapsed time, and per-step profiling breakdown for reports or quick benchmark
notes.

## Physics Profiling

`FluidSolver.step()` records per-step timing and exposes it via the `fluid.stats`
property, which returns a frozen `PhysicsStats` dataclass (`flow_rescue/physics_stats.py`).

### Available fields

| Field | Unit | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `physics_total_ms` | ms | Wall-clock time for the entire `step()` call |
| `grid_build_ms` | ms | Uniform-grid neighbour construction, summed across all PBF iterations |
| `constraint_solve_ms` | ms | Density, lambda, and position-delta kernels, summed across all PBF iterations |
| `collision_ms` | ms | Terrain collision projection during the predict phase |
| `active_particles` | count | Particles marked active after this step |
| `pbf_iterations` | count | Number of PBF solver iterations executed |
| `avg_neighbor_count` | float | Mean neighbour-list length across active particles |
| `grid_overflow` | count | Particles that could not fit in their grid cell |

### Accessing stats

- **Debug panel**: press `T` to show detailed timing lines (hidden by default).
- **Headless mode**: all fields are printed in a `key=value` line for easy parsing by benchmark scripts.
- **Programmatic**: read `fluid.stats` after any `step()` call. The stats are overwritten each step; when multiple sub-steps run per frame, the last step's stats remain.

### Limitations

- Each timing read is preceded by `ti.sync()` to ensure GPU kernels have finished. This
  flushes the command queue on GPU backends and adds a few percent overhead compared to
  unsynced execution.
- `avg_neighbor_count` is computed from host-side numpy data after the final sync, with
  copy overhead proportional to `max_particles`.
- All timing is wall-clock (`time.perf_counter`). On CPU backends the values are accurate;
  on GPU backends they include sync overhead but still correctly measure wall-clock cost.

## Physics Parameters

Core solver knobs are now grouped in `flow_rescue/config.py`:

- `AppConfig.physics`: `max_particles`, `grid_cell_capacity`, `particle_radius`, `smoothing_radius`, `gravity_y`, `velocity_damping`
- `AppConfig.physics.pbf`: `iterations`, `rest_density`, `constraint_epsilon`, `position_relaxation`
- `AppConfig.physics.pbf`: `artificial_pressure_k`, `artificial_pressure_delta_q`
- `AppConfig.physics.viscosity`: `velocity_smoothing`
- `AppConfig.physics.collision`: `query_substeps`, `boundary_epsilon`, `restitution`, `soil_restitution`, `rock_restitution`
- `AppConfig.simulation`: `fixed_dt`, `max_frame_dt`, `max_updates_per_frame`
- `AppConfig.render`: `particle_radius`

These defaults are tuned for the demo's ~480 particles and the CPU-side 2000-particle
stability test. The current defaults also add light velocity smoothing, multi-sample
collision projection, and material-specific restitution to reduce jitter, corner
tunneling, and narrow-channel sticking while keeping rock impacts more responsive than
soft soil impacts.
Future tuning can still refine kernel calibration and density-kernel calibration without
changing the gameplay interface.

For level design workflow and Tiled authoring constraints, see `docs/level_editor.md`.
